head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Computes result^10 mod 1337 in one call (three-argument pow does modular exponentiation without building the huge number)
You need a power modulo m
a^d mod 1337 for one digit d (0 to 9)
Raising a base to a small exponent under a modulus
Multiplies the two parts, then reduces modulo 1337
Reads the digits of b from the most significant to the least significant
Building a number digit by digit

p: If `p` is the number formed by the digits read so far, appending digit `d` makes the number `10 * p + d`. Then `a^(10p + d) = (a^p)^10 * a^d`. `result` always holds `a^p mod 1337`, so one step is `result^10 * a^d`, reduced modulo 1337.

bullets: Time: O(len(b)), each step is a pair of fast modular powers (exponent 10 or at most 9).

372.takeaway: Process the digits of b left to right: the new answer is (old answer)^10 times a^digit, all modulo 1337, so b never has to be turned into a number.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sorts the list in place in ascending order
The answer depends on order statistics such as the median
The middle element (an upper-middle one when the length is even)
Picking the median of a sorted list
Distance from one element to the target value, which is the number of +1/-1 moves it needs
Cost of moving a number to a target
Adds up those distances with a generator expression
Totalling a cost without building a list

blocks.h: Why the median is the best target
p: Take the smallest and the largest element. Together they need at least `max - min` moves to become equal, and any target value between them costs exactly that. So pair up the outermost elements: every pair costs the same for any target inside it. The target that lies inside all pairs is the middle one, the median.

bullets: With an even length, either middle element gives the same total. For `[1, 2, 9, 10]` the target 2 costs `1 + 0 + 7 + 8 = 16` as well.
Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(1) extra (the sort is in place).

462.takeaway: Sort, take the median, and sum the distances to it; the median minimises the total absolute distance.

head: Code
What it does

rows: Each merge removes k - 1 piles, so n piles can become one only if n - 1 is a multiple of k - 1
Prefix sums: pref[j + 1] - pref[i] is the total stones in piles i to j
Minimum cost to merge piles i..j down as far as possible (into one pile when the length fits)

Cost of the left part plus the right part

p: `stones = [3,2,4,1]`, `k = 2`, so `pref = [0,3,5,9,10]`. Every interval can be merged to one pile because `k - 1 = 1`, so the total is always added.
bullets: With `k = 3` the same input has `(4 - 1) % 2 = 1`, so the function returns `-1` at once.

1000.takeaway: Interval DP: the cost of merging piles i..j is the cheapest valid split into two parts, plus the total stones of the interval when it collapses into one pile; check feasibility first with (n - 1) % (k - 1).

No match: skip one number from either side

blocks.h: Why this is the LCS problem
p: Lines that do not cross keep the same left-to-right order on both rows, so the set of connected numbers forms a common subsequence of the two arrays. The most lines equals the length of the Longest Common Subsequence.

1035.takeaway: Non-crossing lines between equal numbers is exactly a longest common subsequence: dp[i][j] = diagonal + 1 on a match, otherwise the larger of the up and left cells.

bullets: For `n = 1010` the loop goes a = 1 (b = 1009 has a 0), 2 (1008), ... 10 (a itself has a 0) and stops at `a = 11`, `b = 999`: it returns `[11, 999]`.
Time: O(n) in the worst case with O(log n) per digit check; in practice a valid pair appears very early.

1317.takeaway: Try a = 1, 2, 3, ...; the partner is n - a, and the first pair where neither number contains a zero digit is the answer.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The leading 1 is handled by the carry at the end
Reads the bits from least significant to most significant
Simulating arithmetic from the low end
The bit plus the carry produced by earlier additions
Adding 1 to a binary number ripples a carry upward
The current number is odd at this position, so add 1 (makes the bit 0 with a carry) then divide: 2 steps
Odd step followed by a shift
The bit is even (0 + 0, or 1 + 1 = 2 which is 0 with a carry), so just divide by 2: 1 step
If a carry is left, the leading 1 became 10 and needs one more halving

p: `s = "1101"` (13). We scan the bits `1, 0, 1` of `s[1:] = "101"` from right to left.
bullets: For `s = "1"` the loop does not run and the answer is `0`.
Space: O(n) for the sliced and reversed copies (O(1) extra beyond that).

1404.takeaway: Simulate the process on the bits from the right: an odd bit (after the carry) costs 2 steps and creates a carry, an even bit costs 1, and a leftover carry adds the last step.

DP (Dynamic Programming) with two values per cell

Boundary handling on the first row and column
The modulus is applied only at the very end, after comparing exact values
Modulo would break comparisons if applied earlier

bullets: Cell (1,1) has value -2: from above `-2 * -2 = 4`, from the left `1 * -2 = -2`, so `hi = 4`, `lo = -2`.
Cell (2,1) has value -4: from above `4 * -4 = -16`, `-2 * -4 = 8`; from the left `3 * -4 = -12`; so `hi = 8`, `lo = -16`.
Space: O(m * n) for the two tables.

1594.takeaway: Keep both the maximum and the minimum product for every cell, because multiplying by a negative number turns the minimum into the maximum; take the modulus only on the final value.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Candidate number of drops, starting from zero
Loops while the triangular number m(m+1)/2 is still too small to cover n floors
A closed-form bound used as a loop test
The smallest m with m(m+1)/2 >= n

p: With `m` drops, the best first drop is at floor `m`. If the egg breaks, the second egg checks floors below one at a time: at most `m - 1` more drops. If it survives, there are `m - 1` drops left, so the next drop goes `m - 1` floors higher, and so on. The floors covered are `m + (m - 1) + ... + 1 = m(m + 1) / 2`.

bullets: Time: O(sqrt(n)), because m grows until m^2 / 2 reaches n.

1884.takeaway: With two eggs and m drops you can cover m + (m-1) + ... + 1 floors, so the answer is the smallest m whose triangular number reaches n.
